crystal.reference: Covington, E. J.; Montgomery, D. J. (1957). Journal of Chemical Physics 27, 1030.
crystal.note: Measured on separated 7Li (natural lithium is mostly 7Li); COD 9012447 gives the 6Li value from the same paper. bcc is the room-temperature form; lithium transforms to close-packed forms on cooling (not covered here).

tonnesPerYear.note: World mine production, lithium content, 2025 (USGS: 290,000 metric tons).

unitValue.note: Price, annual average-real, battery-grade lithium carbonate, dollars per metric ton [Lithium], 2025; per kg of the material named, as USGS gives it.

molarHeatCapacity.note: At 25 °C and 1 bar, per mole of atoms, for the form stable at 25 °C (CRC Handbook, 95th ed.).

uses.text: Rechargeable batteries take almost all of it: 88 % of world use, for electric vehicles, grid storage, electronics and power tools.
Lithium minerals go into ceramics and glass (4 % of world use).
Lubricating greases (2 %); smaller uses are air treatment, fluxes for casting steel, and medicine.

hazardStatements.text: In contact with water releases flammable gases which may ignite spontaneously
Causes severe skin burns and eye damage

origin.note: The paper calls its lithium model 'very uncertain' and leaves out cosmic rays and novae, which make some lithium; its box in Fig. 39 is full to the top, so no split is quoted.

air.text: Stays bright in dry air; in moist air its surface slowly gathers a film of hydroxide, carbonate and nitride.

water.text: Reacts with water, giving lithium hydroxide and hydrogen — the least vigorously of the alkali metals.

compounds.note: used in batteries, glass and as a mood-stabilising drug

compounds.note: lithium is the only alkali metal that reacts with nitrogen at room temperature

biology.note: Not known to be essential for plants or for humans.

history.nameOrigin: From the Greek lithos, 'stone', since it was first found in a mineral (petalite).
history.note: Arfwedson worked in Berzelius's Stockholm laboratory. CIAAW gives 1818. Sources differ on the first isolation of the metal: Jefferson Lab credits electrolysis by Brande and Davy, while CIAAW names Bunsen and Matthiessen (1855), who made it in quantity.

prose.text: Lithium is the lightest metal, a soft, silvery alkali metal that tarnishes quickly in moist air; today we meet it mainly inside the rechargeable batteries of phones and electric cars. With a density of only 0.534 g/cm³ it is the least dense solid element and would float on water, although it reacts with the water as it does so. Its configuration [He] 2s¹ leaves one outer electron alone in the 2s orbital (ground term ²S₁/₂). When that electron is lifted to 2p and falls back, it emits the deep red line near 670.8 nm that colours lithium flames crimson.
